The most accurate difficulty is that the matrix becomes very large and cumbersome to manage.

Wait, let's re-examine the standard chain rule:
$P(A, B, C) = P(A) \cdot P(B | A) \cdot P(C | A, B)$

Let's check if any option matches this form. None of the options exactly match $P(A) \cdot P(B | A) \cdot P(C | A, B)$.

Let's re-examine Option C: $P(C | A, B) \cdot P(A) \cdot P(B)$.
This expression is $P(C | A, B) \cdot P(A, B)$. This is mathematically correct for $P(A, B, C)$.

$P(A, B, C) = P(C | A, B) \cdot P(B | A) \cdot P(A)$.

Let's check the options again. Option C is $P(C | A, B) \cdot P(A) \cdot P(B)$. This is $P(C | A, B) \cdot P(A, B)$. This is a correct representation of the joint probability.
